title: Head injury
subtitle: Who scans, who transfers, who watches

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Head injury: assessment and early management (NG232)
Guidelines for the management of severe traumatic brain injury

red_flags.text: GCS 8 or less, or any fall of 2 or more points sustained for 30 minutes.
A unilateral dilated pupil that is unreactive, or a new lateralising motor deficit.
Cushing response: rising blood pressure with bradycardia and irregular breathing. This is late.
Post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit, or more than one episode of vomiting.
Suspected open or depressed skull fracture, or any sign of a base-of-skull fracture.
Anticoagulated or antiplatelet-treated patient with any head injury, however trivial the mechanism looks.

do_now.text: Airway with cervical spine control. Hypoxia and hypotension each independently worsen outcome in brain injury, and both are preventable.
Capillary glucose in every reduced conscious level, before attributing it to the head injury.
Intubate and ventilate for GCS 8 or less, loss of airway reflexes, or an agitated patient who cannot be scanned safely.
CT head within one hour of identifying any high-risk feature.

assess.text: Record GCS by component and repeat it. A single total conceals the change that matters.
Pupils: size, symmetry, reaction. Document them at the same time as the GCS.
Mechanism, loss of consciousness, amnesia, seizure, vomiting, and any anticoagulation - these five answer the imaging question.
Examine for base-of-skull signs: periorbital or mastoid bruising, cerebrospinal fluid from nose or ear, haemotympanum.
Assume a cervical spine injury in every significant head injury until it is cleared clinically or radiologically.
Score haemorrhage volume and prognosis only after imaging, and only to inform discussion.

investigate.text: CT head, and CT cervical spine when indicated by mechanism, deficit, or an unassessable patient.
Coagulation screen in every anticoagulated patient, with the reversal agent identified before the scan result arrives.
Repeat CT for any unexplained deterioration, or per local policy in an anticoagulated patient with an initially normal scan.
Alcohol and drugs may coexist with an extradural. They are never the explanation until the scan says so.

resuscitate.text: Keep oxygen saturation and blood pressure normal. Avoid hypotension in particular; a single episode is associated with worse outcome.
Nurse head-up at about 30 degrees with the neck neutral and no constricting collar tie, once the spine allows.
Treat pain, agitation and seizures: each raises intracranial pressure. Reverse anticoagulation urgently on the basis of the scan.
Hyperosmolar therapy for signs of herniation, as a bridge to a neurosurgical decision rather than a treatment in itself.

definitive.text: Urgent neurosurgical evacuation for an extradural or acute subdural haematoma with mass effect or a deteriorating patient.
Intracranial pressure monitoring and intensive-care management for severe traumatic brain injury that is not immediately operative.
Observation with a documented neurological observation schedule for the patient with a normal scan and a persistent abnormality of consciousness.
Written head-injury advice, with a named person to stay with them, for anyone discharged.

escalate.text: Discuss every abnormal CT with neurosurgery, including the ones you think need no operation. That conversation is the standard, not a favour.
Transfer intubated, with the scan images available, and with blood pressure and oxygenation stable before the ambulance moves.
An extradural haematoma in a lucid patient is the classic missed catastrophe. Speed of transfer, not speed of investigation, determines outcome.

notes: The two things that turn a survivable brain injury into a poor outcome are hypoxia and hypotension, and both are managed outside the head.
GCS trend beats GCS value. Record the components, record the time, and hand over both.
